subject: disposition
justification: every intended dependency is implied by an adjudicated key and no intended multivalued dependency remains, with no candidate left unruled

subject: author -> author_confidence
justification: confidence belongs to the act of extracting a name from a particular notebook, not to the person named. The same author extracted from a clear byline and from a guess would carry different confidence.

subject: author_confidence,category,notes,score
justification: Textbook accidental composite: two low-cardinality bookkeeping columns (score, author_confidence), a category label, and a mostly-NULL free-text column (notes: 14 distinct values, 27 NULLs). None of these identifies anything. The combination is 39/49 distinct, so it is near-unique by chance in a 49-row table. Of the 7 combinations that repeat, 6 are satisfied trivially because the author_confidence='unknown' component already restricts author to NULL/'unknown' and those groups happen to be internally homogeneous; the sole remaining group is one accidental cluster of three Karl Scherer rows sharing (extracted, direct_tiling_source, NULL, 8). Note also that author_confidence alone does NOT determine author (NULL and 'unknown' both occur under it), which is precisely why the FD has to drag in three unrelated columns to reach uniqueness. Approving this would model 'a score plus a category plus a note identifies a person', which is false.

subject: original_filename -> author_confidence
justification: a filename is a label. Category and score are judgements recorded about the notebook and are not fixed by what the file was called.

subject: title
justification: title is free text and 48/49 distinct - the canonical near-unique-column tell. It 'determines everything' because it almost never repeats, and its single repeat (ids 2 and 31, the same notebook ingested twice) supplies one row of evidence that itself contradicts the pattern by disagreeing on reason, author and notes. Ownership also runs the wrong way: title is derived from original_filename (45/49 exact slug decode), so title -> original_filename is the inverse of the real rule and is not recoverable in the domain - the filename's version segment (1-0-0, 2-0-0, 7-0-1, 10-0-0) and the '(1)' ingest-duplicate marker are not present in the title, and the slug transform is lossy (apostrophes, diacritics). Finally, score and category are curator judgements recorded per catalog row; a title string cannot own them. Nothing here is a property of the modelled world.

subject: model
value: One curated notebook file copy currently held under .local/notebooks (in notebook-sources/ or notebook-sources3/), carrying its triage score, category, rationale, attributed author, and the path it was ingested from.
justification: DDL declares `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` and `filename TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE`; the unique index (sqlite_autoindex_notebooks_1) is enforced and NOT NULL closes SQLite's NULL loophole, so both identify a row. A row is one catalogued file copy, not one notebook work: ids 2 and 31 share title and original_filename while living in notebook-sources/ and notebook-sources3/, and both files exist today. That single pair is the sole source of the reported title/original_filename BCNF and 2NF violations, so neither is a key. Remaining open uniqueness subjects are accidental at n=49: reason and notes are bespoke free text; author,* and notes,* pairings lean on nullable columns (27 NULL notes); original_path is frozen ingest provenance that repeats legally if one source is ingested twice (27 of 49 original_paths no longer exist); relative_path uniqueness is a theorem of UNIQUE(filename), since relative_path = directory + '/' + filename. Scope is current-state: all 49 relative_paths resolve on disk, and 27 files in notebook-sources plus 22 in notebook-sources3 equal the 49 rows exactly. No builder exists on this machine, so not per-build; with no content-hash column nothing rebinds over time, so not historical.
